text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG

- German federation, states and communes in 18 billion tax shortfall. Germany will also have to reckon with some 32 billion marks less tax income for 1998. But the government is seeking to plug the gaps without tax increases and without too severe spending cuts. Finance minister Waigel however continues to reserve his right to impose a spending freeze on government departments.

- Opposition German politicians call for Waigel to step down due to the harsh savings programme required by his continued insistence on a strict interpretation of economic criteria for entry into the single European currency.
- German prosecutors issue arrest warrants for three Iranian intelligence officers over the 1992 killing of four Iranian Kurish dissidents in Berlin.

- U.S. President Clinton says Russia may be granted a vote in decisions over NATO business but will have no right of veto. Likely new NATO members Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary, will probably not be the last, Clinton says in Washington.
- EU finance ministers preparing to take action to ensure that expected turbulence on foreign currency markets next year does not endanger the arrival of the euro a year later.
- Finance minister Waigel plans upward reevaluation of Bundesbank gold reserves for 1997 budgetary purposes.
HANDELSBLATT

- Waigel asserts that not one ounce of Bundesbank gold will be sold in the light of news that German tax receipts will be sharply down on previous expectations. But the tax shortfall has opened up a range of political divisions on what to do about it.
- Deutsche Bahn railways supervisory board approves the new consortium plan to build the Transrapid high-speed magnetic levitation rail project.
- Sale of the Berlin publicly-held utility Bewag under threat from veto by the Federal Cartel Office.
- China rewards French prime minister Chirac with billion-franc orders after France's change of human rights policy on China and a ban on arms trade with Taiwan.
- British Telecom says well-positioned for international markets as presents its 1996/97 results.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- 18 billion mark gap opens up in German budget with new 1997 tax estimate
- Germany's health insurance schemes assess their response to government demands for cost-cutting that will not however impact patients suffering serious illnesses or needing urgent care.
- Insurance companies increasingly concerned about the potentially catastrophic" effects of overcrowding in inner cities.
DIE WELT
- Finance minister Waigel on the search for new ways to raise money after 18 billion mark shortfall in 1997 tax estimates
- Government in row over possible rise in petrol tax, with junior coalition partners the FDP anxious to rule out any increase that its parnters might be considering.
- Rape in marriage finally outlawed, pubishable by at least a two-year prison sentence.
- South African mediators lay out peace plan to avoid possible bloodbath in Zaire, based on draft proposals for transition government.
- Newly-announced Lufthansa "Star Alliance" will aim to extend coverage to small destinations never before reached within major airline network.
- A new law envisaging greater competition in Germany's postal system could encounter hostility in the upper house of German parliament on Friday.
